title: Biology as Code: an open, provenance-tracked toolkit for meal digestion and metabolic-pathway modeling
description:
biology-as-code is an open-source Python package that models what happens to a meal — digestion, absorption, and the metabolic pathways it drives — as inspectable code rather than a numeric verdict. It fails closed: where a required fact is not declared it returns UNEVALUABLE rather than a default pass, a zero, or an interpolated estimate.

It provides a meal-simulation pipeline, the gastrointestinal tract as versioned declarative state machines, 28 teaching metabolic-pathway graphs, 47 LAW-SPEC law cards expressing rules as queryable data, a typed food-packet loader, and a claim auditor that walks a nutrition claim through the L1–L5 delivery ladder and returns a verdict with citations to the laws it rests on. Gate (categorical) and bound (signed magnitude) are separated at the type level, and continuous integration asserts that a gate rule may only cite laws whose card declares a gate.

Pure Python (≥3.11), dependency-free at runtime, no network calls by default. FLOW teaching and research software; not medical advice. The patent-pending product scoring engine is deliberately not included — see PROPRIETARY_IP.md. Validation tiers are documented in docs/VALIDATION.md.

This release also publishes FDP-1, the Food Data Provenance Declaration — a minimal, RFC-style specification for declaring the provenance grade of a nutrient value (six fields) and the validation status of any score computed from such values (five fields, incl. a weakest-link provenance rule). FDP-1 wraps any existing scoring system (Nutri-Score, Health Star Rating, Nutri-Grade, Food Compass, or proprietary scores) without modification. Shipped with a dependency-free reference validator, the MASTER_CROSSWALK ID spine, and a worked two-host iron example. A patent non-assertion covenant applies to the open layer (see PATENTS.md).

On the name: unrelated to Code Biology (Barbieri and others), which studies organic codes in living systems. The claim here is methodological rather than semiotic: nutrition and pathway models should be written like software.
